transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You found the friction force correctly. Can you check if the normal force is really just mg on an incline?
Oh, is it not just mg? Does the angle go in there somehow?
Okay, let me think.
Good question. On an incline, the normal force is less than mg because the surface only supports part of the weight.
So is it mg times cos 30 or mg times sin 30?
Good question. One moment.
Good question—on an incline, the normal force is mg times cos 30, not sin 30.
Okay so N is 49 times cos 30, 42.4, and friction is 0.2 times that, 8.5 N. But why cos and not sin?
Let me see.
You're right about the normal force being mg cos 30, and the friction being μ times that. The cosine comes from the component of weight perpendicular to the incline.
But why is the perpendicular part cos? Why isn't the perpendicular one sin?
Got it. Give me a second.
The cosine gives the adjacent side in the right triangle formed by the weight vector and the incline.
Adjacent to what though? Which angle is 30 in that triangle? I can't picture it.
Okay, let me think.
The 30-degree angle is between the incline and the horizontal. The weight vector points straight down, so the adjacent side to that angle is the perpendicular component.
But the 30 is down at the bottom of the ramp, not by the weight arrow. How is it in that triangle?
Good question. One moment.
The 30-degree angle is between the incline and the horizontal, so it's the same angle in the right triangle formed by the weight vector.
Why is it the same angle though? You're just saying it is.
Let me see.
The angle is the same because the incline and the horizontal form a right triangle with the weight vector.
I still don't really get why it's cos. I'll just use 8.5 N I guess.
Got it. Give me a second.
You're using the wrong normal force. On an incline, N is mg cos 30, not mg. Try that and see what you get.
